title: Saint Thomas Aquinas
orientation: This chapter gives Russell's extended exposition and critique of Thomas Aquinas, whom the Catholic Church has held to be the definitive Christian philosopher since Leo XIII's 1879 rescript. It matters because Aquinas's systematic fusion of Aristotle with Christian doctrine, above all in the Summa contra Gentiles, remains a living philosophical system studied and taught today, and because Russell's critique of it -- that its conclusions are fixed in advance and its 'reason' therefore not fully sincere -- exemplifies his general standard for what counts as genuine philosophy.
historical_background: Aquinas (1225/1226-1274), son of the Count of Aquino, was educated near Monte Cassino, studied at Frederick II's university of Naples, became a Dominican, and studied under Albertus Magnus (the leading Aristotelian of the age) at Cologne. He spent most of his career in Italy and Paris, where, during 1269-72, the Dominicans' Aristotelianism made them suspect of sympathy with the Averroists, who held (against Catholic doctrine) that only an impersonal intellect, not the individual soul, survives death. Aquinas, uniquely well-informed on Aristotle thanks to William of Moerbeke's fresh translations from the Greek, worked to establish a purified, non-Averroist, non-Neoplatonized Aristotle as the philosophical basis of Christian orthodoxy -- a project so successful that Aristotle acquired, among Catholics, 'almost the authority of one of the Fathers.'
philosophical_problems: Can natural reason, independent of revelation, prove the existence of God and other religious truths, and if so, which truths (and which not)?
Is the ontological argument for God's existence valid, and if not, what other arguments succeed?
Can God know particular, contingent things, or only universals -- and if the former, how, given that particulars are material, changeable, and (for future contingents) not yet existent?
What is the relationship between the soul and the intellect in human beings, and is each person's intellect individually distinct (against Averroes)?
Whether an infinite regress in a causal series is truly impossible, and whether this can ground a valid proof of a First Cause
Whether rational ethical argument (e.g. concerning marriage, sexuality, poverty) can be sincerely pursued when its conclusions are fixed in advance by doctrine

philosophers_discussed.name: Thomas Aquinas
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's central subject: a Dominican friar and the greatest scholastic philosopher, whose Summa contra Gentiles and Summa Theologiae synthesize Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine; Russell gives an extended abstract of the Summa contra Gentiles' four books before offering a sustained critical assessment.

philosophers_discussed.name: Albertus Magnus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Aquinas's teacher at Cologne, described as the leading Aristotelian philosopher of the time, under whom Aquinas studied after becoming a Dominican.

philosophers_discussed.name: Averroes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Referenced as the source of the 'Averroist' doctrine (denial of individual immortality, since only impersonal intellect survives) that Aquinas worked in Paris to refute and separate Aristotle from; Aquinas explicitly denies Averroes's claim that there is only one intellect shared among all men.

philosophers_discussed.name: David of Dinant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: An early thirteenth-century materialistic pantheist whom Aquinas rejects for 'raving' that God is the same as primary matter, since God is pure activity while primary matter is pure passivity.

schools_discussed: Averroism (the doctrine, opposed by Aquinas, of a single impersonal intellect shared by all humans)

core_concepts.name: The five (and related) proofs of God's existence
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aquinas offers several arguments that God exists, most turning on the idea that an endless backward chain of causes or changes is impossible, so there must be a first, uncaused cause or unmoved mover. The unmoved mover argument says: things that move are moved by something else; since this chain can't go back forever, there must be something that moves everything else without itself being moved -- this is God. Related arguments run the same way for causes generally, for the source of necessity, and add arguments from degrees of perfection in the world (there must be something maximally perfect as their source) and from the apparent purposiveness even of lifeless things (which must be directed by something outside themselves, since only living things have internal purposes).
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aquinas's cosmological-style arguments (the unmoved mover, the first cause, the ultimate source of necessity, the argument from degrees of perfection, and the argument from design/purposiveness in lifeless things) for God's existence, presented in the Summa contra Gentiles and, in a fuller five-fold form, the Summa Theologiae; contrasted with, and explicitly preferred by Aquinas over, the ontological argument.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: These arguments are the foundational rational case for theism within the Thomistic system, and remain influential and widely taught within Catholic philosophy to the present day per Church teaching following Leo XIII's 1879 rescript.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Aquinas, adapting and Christianizing Aristotle's own argument for an unmoved mover, in the Summa contra Gentiles (1259-64) and Summa Theologiae.
examples: Russell's footnote that in Aristotle's own version, the unmoved-mover argument actually leads to 47 or 55 Gods, not one
The argument that lifeless things serving a purpose must be directed by something outside themselves, since only living things can have an internal purpose
objections: Russell's central objection: all of the arguments except the design argument depend on the supposed impossibility of a series having no first term, but 'every mathematician knows there is no such impossibility' -- the series of negative integers ending in minus one is a counterexample
competing_positions: The ontological argument (rejected by Aquinas himself, on the grounds that we do not know God's essence well enough to deduce His existence from it)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Remains, per Russell, unshakeable in practice among believers regardless of the arguments' logical soundness, since 'no Catholic is likely to abandon belief in God even if he becomes convinced that Saint Thomas's arguments are bad; he will invent other arguments, or take refuge in revelation.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to Catholic doctrine and, since 1879, mandatory teaching in Catholic educational institutions.

core_concepts.name: The rejection of the ontological argument
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Some thinkers said God's existence is self-evident once we understand what 'God' means. Aquinas disagrees: that would only work if we knew God's essence perfectly, since (he holds) in God essence and existence are identical -- but no creature, however wise, knows God's essence well enough to deduce His existence purely from the concept. So the existence of God needs a separate proof, not a definitional shortcut.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aquinas's argument that the ontological proof (deriving God's existence from the concept of God) fails because, although essence and existence are indeed identical in God Himself, no finite intellect grasps God's essence with sufficient completeness to perform this deduction.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It shows Aquinas deliberately choosing cosmological over a priori argumentation, a methodological choice that shaped the subsequent Thomistic tradition's preference for arguments from the created world over pure conceptual analysis.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Presented early in Book I of the Summa contra Gentiles, following the treatment of the nature of wisdom.
examples: Aquinas's distinction between wise men, the ignorant, and angels as knowing progressively more of God's essence, yet none sufficiently to deduce existence from it
competing_positions: Saint Anselm's ontological argument (covered in the chapter on the eleventh century), which Aquinas here implicitly rejects
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Establishes the cosmological-argument tradition within Catholic philosophy as against the ontological-argument tradition later revived by Descartes and Leibniz.

core_concepts.name: God's knowledge of particulars
core_concepts.plain_explanation: If God only knows general truths and universals, not this particular person or event, that seems to threaten the Christian doctrine of Providence (which requires God to know and care about individual lives). But there are serious objections: particulars are made of 'signate matter,' which an immaterial being seemingly cannot know; particulars come in and out of existence, which seems incompatible with the unchanging character of divine knowledge; some particulars are contingent, not necessary, so it seems they cannot be certainly known in advance; and particulars are infinite in number, seemingly beyond any finite grasp. Aquinas answers that God knows particulars as their cause (much as a maker knows what he is making), that God sees all times as an eternal present rather than in temporal sequence, that He knows our minds directly, and that nothing is truly 'trivial' since the order of the universe as a whole is noble and cannot be known without knowing its parts.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aquinas's resolution, in Book I of the Summa contra Gentiles, of seven objections to the claim that God has knowledge of individual, contingent, and even seemingly trivial or evil particulars, arguing that God's causal, atemporal mode of knowing avoids all seven difficulties.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This question, which Russell notes 'had already troubled both Plato and Aristotle,' is essential to reconciling divine omniscience with Christian Providence, free will, and the moral significance of individual human lives.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Treated systematically by Aquinas in Summa contra Gentiles, Book I.
examples: The seven objections Aquinas enumerates and then answers, including that singulars are 'too petty for God's attention' and that 'in some singulars there is evil, but God cannot know evil'
Aquinas's reply that God knows evil because knowing any good involves knowing its opposite
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly grounds the Christian doctrine of Providence.

core_concepts.name: The individual human soul, intellect, and the rejection of Averroism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aquinas holds each person has exactly one soul (not three, as some earlier theories held), which is the 'form' of the body, present entirely in every part of it, and created fresh by God for each individual rather than transmitted through the parents (unlike, say, physical traits). Crucially, and against Averroes, each person's intellect is likewise their own, individual and distinct -- not a single impersonal intellect in which all people merely participate. This matters because only individual immortality, not Averroes's shared impersonal intellect, secures the Christian doctrine of personal survival and judgment after death.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aquinas's doctrine, contra Averroes, that the intellectual part of each human soul is numerically distinct for each individual, immaterial and incorruptible, created directly by God (not transmitted through generation), and hence capable of grounding genuine personal immortality.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is the doctrinal crux of the Averroist controversy at thirteenth-century Paris, and Aquinas's decisive rejection of the single-intellect view was central to the Church's condemnation of Latin Averroism.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in Book II of the Summa contra Gentiles as part of Aquinas's broader account of the soul.
examples: The objection Aquinas considers and dismisses as merely 'specious': that if the soul is created afresh rather than transmitted with the semen, an illegitimately conceived child's ensoulment seems to implicate God as an 'accomplice in adultery'
Russell's aside that Aquinas does not discuss the harder, related problem (which troubled Saint Augustine) of how, if each soul is created fresh, it can inherit Adam's original sin
objections: Russell's own view, stated directly, that 'the De Anima leads much more naturally to the view of Averroes than to that of Aquinas'
competing_positions: Averroes's view that intellect is one and impersonal, shared across all human beings
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Secured the Church's decisive rejection of Averroism as heretical, shaping subsequent Catholic psychology and eschatology.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Underwrites the doctrine of personal judgment and individual salvation.

arguments.title: The argument of the unmoved mover
premises: There are things which are only moved, and other things which both move and are moved
Whatever is moved is moved by something else
An endless regress of movers is impossible
arguments.conclusion: There must be something that moves other things without itself being moved by anything; this unmoved mover is God.
arguments.explanation: Aquinas addresses the objection that this argument presupposes the eternity of motion (which Catholics reject as unorthodox), replying that the argument holds equally well, and is even strengthened, on the alternative hypothesis that motion had a beginning, since a beginning itself implies a First Cause.
objections: Russell's general objection to this whole family of arguments: the supposed impossibility of a series without a first term is false, since mathematics provides counterexamples, e.g. the series of negative integers ending at minus one
implications: Russell notes that in Aristotle's own original version, applied literally to the planetary spheres, the same style of argument yields 47 or 55 unmoved movers, not one God

arguments.title: The five ways of the Summa Theologiae
premises: The impossibility of an infinite regress of efficient causes (the First Cause argument)
The need for an ultimate source of all necessity
The presence of varying degrees of perfection in the world, which must derive from something completely perfect
The observed purposiveness even of lifeless things, which (since only living things have internal purposes) must be directed by an external being
arguments.conclusion: God exists, established independently by five converging arguments.
arguments.explanation: Russell lists all five as given in the Summa Theologiae, noting the second and third are 'much the same' as each other and closely related to the first.
objections: The same infinite-regress objection applies to the first three of the five ways

arguments.title: Aquinas's resolution of the seven objections to God's knowledge of particulars
premises: God knows particulars as their cause, the way an artificer knows what he is making before it exists
God sees all times, including future contingents, as an eternal present rather than experiencing succession
God knows all minds and secret wills directly
Nothing is genuinely trivial, since the order of the universe as a whole is noble and cannot be known without knowing its parts
Knowledge of any good necessarily involves knowledge of its corresponding evil
arguments.conclusion: God can and does know particular, contingent, infinite, seemingly trivial, and even evil things, consistent with His unchanging, immaterial nature.
arguments.explanation: Each premise answers one or more of the seven objections Aquinas raises against divine knowledge of particulars (that singularity is signate matter unknowable to the immaterial, that singulars don't always exist, that they are contingent not necessary, that some depend on private volitions, that they are infinite in number, that they are too petty, and that some involve evil).
implications: Secures the doctrine of divine Providence, which requires God to know and act upon particular events and choices

key_distinctions: Truths of faith demonstrable by natural reason (God's existence, immortality of the soul) vs. truths knowable only by revelation (the Trinity, the Incarnation, the Last Judgement)
God's essence (which we do not know sufficiently) vs. God's existence (which is provable, per Aquinas, though not via the ontological argument)
Universale ante rem (in God's mind before creation) vs. universale post rem (abstracted by human understanding after experience) -- Aquinas allows only the latter for explaining human knowledge
The soul as the 'form' of the body (Aristotelian) vs. Platonic/Averroist views of the soul-body or intellect relation
Reason (the first three books of the Summa contra Gentiles) vs. revelation (reserved chiefly for the fourth book, on Trinity, Incarnation, papal supremacy, sacraments, and resurrection)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Aquinas's whole philosophical framework is explicitly Aristotelian, secured by his friend William of Moerbeke's fresh Greek-to-Latin translations, which allowed Aquinas -- unlike his scholastic predecessors -- genuine, undistorted access to Aristotle free of the Neoplatonic overlay traced through earlier chapters (Kindi, Avicenna); his rejection of Averroes's single-intellect doctrine directly continues the debate introduced in Chapter X.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Aquinas's cosmological arguments remain foundational to later natural theology; Russell notes his own critique -- that positing an identity of essence and existence in God 'suggests a confusion, found in Plato, but supposed to have been avoided by Aristotle, between the manner of being of particulars and the manner of being of universals' -- points forward to the logical/linguistic critiques of scholastic metaphysics that Russell associates with modern analytic philosophy.
political_social_context: Since Pope Leo XIII's 1879 rescript, Aquinas's system has been mandatory teaching in all Catholic educational institutions, making him, in Russell's words, not merely of historical interest but 'a living influence, like Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and Hegel'; Russell notes personally that criticizing Aquinas 'in matters of pure philosophy has come to be thought almost impious' among Catholics, adding a footnote that a broadcast in which he did so 'resulted' in 'very many protests from Catholics.'
religion_science_culture_context: Aquinas's ethical arguments (on marriage, celibacy, monogamy, incest, and voluntary poverty) are presented as appeals to 'purely rational considerations,' with scriptural citation typically added only after a conclusion in harmony with Christian teaching has already been reached by reasoning; Russell treats this pattern as symptomatic of his broader critique that Thomistic 'reason' is not fully sincere, since its conclusions are fixed by doctrine in advance.
russell_presentation: Russell credits Aquinas with genuine intellectual virtues: unusually competent, direct knowledge of Aristotle; sharp and admirable clarity in distinguishing arguments from reason and arguments from revelation; systematic power sufficient to make the Summa 'an imposing intellectual edifice' even if every individual doctrine in it were mistaken; and real fairness in stating opposing views before refuting them. But Russell's overall verdict, stated with unusual directness at the chapter's close, is severely critical: he denies Aquinas 'the true philosophic spirit,' arguing that because Aquinas already knows the truth in advance (it is given by Catholic faith) and merely seeks supporting arguments -- falling back on revelation if reason fails -- his method is 'not philosophy, but special pleading,' and he 'does not deserve to be put on a level with the best philosophers either of Greece or of modern times.' Russell illustrates the alleged insincerity of Aquinas's 'rational' arguments with the marriage-indissolubility case and with the cosmological arguments' shared, mathematically unsound premise about infinite regress.
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism: Thomist philosophers have long disputed Russell's central charge that Aquinas's arguments are insincere 'special pleading,' arguing instead that reaching a conclusion already held on other grounds (faith) does not by itself invalidate an independent rational demonstration of the same conclusion; some also argue Russell's brief 'negative integers' counterexample to the impossibility-of-infinite-regress premise does not fully engage with Aquinas's distinction between an essentially ordered (per se) causal series, to which the argument is meant to apply, and an accidentally ordered (per accidens) series like the integers, where it is not.
key_takeaways: Since Leo XIII's 1879 rescript, Aquinas's philosophy is mandatory teaching in Catholic educational institutions, making him a 'living influence' rather than merely a historical figure.

Aquinas's Summa contra Gentiles divides religious truths into those provable by natural reason (God's existence, soul's immortality) and those knowable only by revelation (Trinity, Incarnation, Last Judgement), confining rational argument to the first three of its four books.

Aquinas rejects the ontological argument (we cannot know God's essence well enough to deduce existence from it) in favor of cosmological arguments from motion, causation, necessity, degrees of perfection, and purposiveness.
Against Averroes, Aquinas holds that each human being's intellect is individually distinct, not a single impersonal intellect shared by all -- essential to securing personal immortality.

Aquinas resolves seven objections to claim that God can know particular, contingent, even trivial or evil things, chiefly by holding that God knows particulars as their cause and sees all times as an eternal present.

Russell's ultimate verdict is sharply critical: because Aquinas's conclusions are fixed in advance by faith, his 'rational' arguments amount to special pleading rather than genuine philosophical inquiry, notwithstanding his real systematic and expository skill.
study_notes:
The chapter has a clear two-part structure worth studying separately: first, a long, mostly neutral abstract of the Summa contra Gentiles (covering wisdom, the proofs of God, the divine attributes, God's knowledge and will, creation, the soul, ethics, providence, and finally the fourth book's revealed doctrines); second, a compact but pointed critical assessment at the very end (continuing into the opening of the next chapter). Read the abstract section for content -- what Aquinas actually argues -- and the closing section for Russell's method of evaluation, which is worth extracting as a general pattern: Russell distinguishes real philosophical merit (clarity, fairness to opponents, systematic thoroughness, genuine command of Aristotle) from what he considers philosophical insincerity (reasoning toward a conclusion fixed in advance).

Pay special attention to the cosmological arguments and Russell's single central objection to them -- the mathematical counterexample to 'a series must have a first term' -- since this is the clearest instance in the chapter of Russell deploying a specifically logical/mathematical tool (rather than a purely historical or theological one) to assess a piece of medieval argumentation, characteristic of his own philosophical style.

Finally, notice how the chapter quietly continues the Averroist thread from Chapter X: Aquinas's insistence on individually distinct intellects is not an abstract metaphysical preference but a direct response to the specific doctrine (shared impersonal intellect, no personal immortality) that had made Averroism dangerous at Paris. Russell's own aside -- that he thinks the De Anima actually supports Averroes's reading better than Aquinas's -- is a good example of Russell distinguishing historical exposition (what Aquinas argued and why the Church accepted it) from his own independent judgment about the underlying interpretive question.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aquinas's major work (1259-64) arguing for the truth of Christianity using reasons that do not presuppose the reader already accepts Christian revelation.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A four-book systematic work by Aquinas addressed to an imagined reader versed in Arabic philosophy but not already Christian; the first three books rely on natural reason, while the fourth treats doctrines (Trinity, Incarnation, sacraments, resurrection) knowable only through revelation.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that behind every chain of things causing other things to move, there must be one first thing that starts the motion without itself being moved by anything else -- and this, for Aquinas, is God.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aquinas's adaptation of Aristotle's argument that an infinite regress of movers is impossible, requiring a first mover that is itself unmoved, identified with God; the first and most emphasized of Aquinas's proofs of God's existence.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The claim that God's existence can be proven just from understanding the concept of God, without needing any other evidence.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The a priori argument (associated with Anselm) that God's existence follows from His definition as the being than which none greater can be conceived; Aquinas rejects it on the grounds that human beings do not know God's essence with sufficient completeness to perform this deduction.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view, drawn from Averroes, that only an impersonal, shared intellect survives death -- meaning individual people do not have personal immortality.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The thirteenth-century Parisian doctrine, attributed to Averroes's interpretation of Aristotle's De Anima, that intellect is numerically one and impersonal across all human beings, denying individual personal immortality; explicitly rejected by Aquinas in favor of individually distinct souls/intellects.
related_concepts: Individual human soul, intellect, and the rejection of Averroism

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A scholastic term for the specific matter that makes a particular thing this individual thing rather than another of the same kind.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In scholastic terminology, matter as marked out or individuated by specific quantitative dimensions, invoked in the objection that an immaterial being (like God) cannot know particulars, since particularity is constituted by signate matter.

questions.prompt: What is the structural division of the Summa contra Gentiles into truths provable by reason and truths knowable only by revelation, and how does this division map onto its four books?
questions.answer: The first three books make no essential appeal to revelation (except to show conclusions reached by reason agree with it); only the fourth book, on the Trinity, the Incarnation, papal supremacy, the sacraments, and the resurrection, treats matters that cannot be known apart from revelation. Natural reason can prove God's existence and the soul's immortality, but not the Trinity, Incarnation, or Last Judgement.
questions.explanation: This division reflects Aquinas's stated view that revelation and reason are both valid but distinct sources of religious knowledge, with reason's scope explicitly limited.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Aquinas's unmoved mover argument for God's existence, and state Russell's central objection to it.
questions.answer: The argument: some things are only moved while others both move and are moved; whatever is moved is moved by something else; since an endless regress of movers is impossible, there must be a first, unmoved mover, identified with God. Russell's objection: the premise that a series must have a first term is false -- mathematics provides counterexamples, such as the series of negative integers ending at minus one -- undermining the argument's key premise.
questions.explanation: Russell notes this objection applies to several of Aquinas's proofs, since most (all but the design argument) rest on the same impossibility-of-infinite-regress premise.

questions.prompt: Why does Aquinas reject the ontological argument for God's existence?
questions.answer: Because while it is true that in God, essence and existence are identical (making the argument valid in principle if we knew God's essence), no creature -- however wise, even angels -- knows God's essence completely enough to be able to deduce His existence from it. So the ontological shortcut fails in practice, even though its underlying premise about God is one Aquinas accepts.
questions.explanation: This shows Aquinas endorsing the metaphysical premise behind Anselm's argument while denying we have epistemic access sufficient to run the inference.

questions.prompt: How does Aquinas resolve the difficulty that God's knowledge of particulars seems incompatible with His unchanging, immaterial, eternal nature?
questions.answer: Aquinas argues God knows particulars as their cause (as a maker knows what he is making, even before it exists), knows future contingents because He sees all of time as an eternal present rather than experiencing succession, knows minds and secret wills directly, and knows even trivial or evil things because nothing is wholly trivial (the noble order of the universe requires knowing its parts) and knowing any good entails knowing its corresponding evil.
questions.explanation: This answers all seven objections Aquinas himself raises against divine knowledge of particulars.

questions.prompt: Compare Aquinas's view of the individual human intellect with that of Averroes.
questions.answer: Averroes held that intellect (nous) is one and impersonal, shared identically across all human beings, so that while intellect itself is immortal, no individual person achieves personal immortality. Aquinas rejects this: he holds each person's intellect is their own, individually created afresh by God (not transmitted through generation), immaterial and incorruptible -- securing genuine personal immortality, consistent with Christian doctrine on judgment and salvation.
questions.explanation: Russell notes his own view that the De Anima actually supports Averroes's reading better than Aquinas's, even though the Church has followed Aquinas since his time.

questions.prompt: What is Russell's central criticism of Aquinas's overall philosophical method, stated at the chapter's close?
questions.answer: Russell argues Aquinas lacks the 'true philosophic spirit' because he does not, like the Platonic Socrates, follow the argument wherever it leads; instead, he already knows the truth in advance (given by Catholic faith), and merely seeks rational arguments to support it -- falling back on revelation if reason fails. Russell calls this 'not philosophy, but special pleading,' and concludes Aquinas does not deserve to be ranked with the best philosophers of Greece or modern times.
questions.explanation: This judgment, though harsh, follows directly from examples given earlier in the chapter, such as the indissolubility-of-marriage argument, where Russell notes no Thomist would actually abandon the conclusion even if the stated reasons were refuted.

questions.prompt: Give Russell's example of how Aquinas's 'rational' ethical arguments are not fully sincere, using the case of marriage.
questions.answer: Aquinas argues marriage should be lifelong because the father is useful in educating children, being more rational than the mother and physically stronger for administering punishment. Russell notes a modern educator could reasonably reject both premises, but that no follower of Aquinas would, on that account, abandon belief in lifelong monogamy -- showing the real grounds of the belief are not the stated rational arguments.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this as his clearest illustration of the broader charge that Thomistic reasoning is insincere because its conclusions are fixed independently of the arguments offered for them.

flashcards.front: What are Aquinas's dates, and what order did he join?
flashcards.back: b. 1225 or 1226, d. 1274; joined the Dominican order.

flashcards.front: Since what event has Aquinas's system been mandatory teaching in Catholic educational institutions?
flashcards.back: A 1879 rescript by Pope Leo XIII.

flashcards.front: Who was Aquinas's teacher at Cologne, and how is he described?
flashcards.back: Albertus Magnus, described as the leading Aristotelian philosopher of the time.

flashcards.front: What are Aquinas's two major works discussed in this chapter?
flashcards.back: Summa contra Gentiles (1259-64) and Summa Theologiae.

flashcards.front: What two categories of religious truth does Aquinas distinguish?
flashcards.back: Truths demonstrable by natural reason (e.g. God's existence, soul's immortality) and truths knowable only by revelation (e.g. Trinity, Incarnation, Last Judgement).

flashcards.front: Why does Aquinas reject the ontological argument?
flashcards.back: Because although essence and existence are identical in God, no creature knows God's essence well enough to deduce His existence from it.

flashcards.front: State the unmoved mover argument in one sentence.
flashcards.back: Since an infinite regress of movers is impossible, there must be a first, unmoved mover -- God.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's key objection to the infinite-regress premise in Aquinas's cosmological arguments?
flashcards.back: It is mathematically false: the series of negative integers ending at minus one is a series with no first term, contradicting the premise.

flashcards.front: What is David of Dinant's error, according to Aquinas?
flashcards.back: Claiming God is the same as primary matter; Aquinas rejects this because primary matter is pure passivity while God is pure activity.

flashcards.front: Against Averroes, what does Aquinas hold about each person's intellect?
flashcards.back: That it is individually distinct and created afresh by God for each person, not a single impersonal intellect shared by all.

flashcards.front: How does Aquinas resolve the objection that God's knowledge would require knowing 'petty' or trivial things?
flashcards.back: Nothing is wholly trivial; the noble order of the universe as a whole cannot be known without knowing even its small parts.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's final verdict on Aquinas's philosophical status?
flashcards.back: That he lacks the true philosophic spirit, since his conclusions are fixed in advance by faith, making his arguments 'special pleading' rather than genuine philosophy.

flashcards.front: What example does Russell use to show Aquinas's ethical reasoning is not fully sincere?
flashcards.back: The indissolubility of marriage: even if the stated rational arguments (father's superior rationality and strength) were refuted, no Thomist would abandon the conclusion.

flashcards.front: What curious theological puzzle does Aquinas resolve concerning cannibalism and bodily resurrection?
flashcards.back: He argues bodily identity does not depend on retaining the same matter (since digestion constantly replaces bodily matter during life), so a cannibal can receive the same body at the resurrection even without the same matter he died with.

quiz.explanation: Aquinas rejects the ontological argument, on the ground that we do not know God's essence well enough to deduce His existence from it, despite accepting that essence and existence are identical in God.
quiz.related_concept: The rejection of the ontological argument

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's central objection to Aquinas's cosmological arguments (unmoved mover, first cause, source of necessity)?
options: They are not based on Aristotle
They rest on the false premise that a series must have a first term, which mathematics disproves
They contradict Church doctrine
They were never actually written by Aquinas
quiz.explanation: Russell notes every mathematician knows there is no such impossibility, citing the series of negative integers ending at minus one as a counterexample.
quiz.related_concept: The five (and related) proofs of God's existence

quiz.prompt: Against which doctrine, associated with Averroes, does Aquinas argue that each individual's intellect is distinct?
options: The doctrine that the soul does not exist
The doctrine that intellect is one and impersonal, shared across all human beings
The doctrine that only angels have intellect
The doctrine that animals have immortal souls
quiz.explanation: Averroism held intellect to be a single, impersonal faculty shared by all people, denying personal immortality; Aquinas insists each person's intellect is individually distinct and created afresh by God.
quiz.related_concept: The individual human soul, intellect, and the rejection of Averroism

quiz.prompt: According to Aquinas, God knows future contingents because He sees all of time as an eternal ____ rather than experiencing succession.
options: present
past
cycle
void
quiz.explanation: Aquinas resolves the puzzle of God's knowledge of future contingents by holding that God, being outside time, sees each moment as if present.

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's ultimate verdict on whether Aquinas deserves to be ranked among the greatest philosophers?
options: Russell ranks him above Plato and Aristotle
Russell denies him the 'true philosophic spirit,' since his conclusions are fixed in advance by faith, making his method 'special pleading' rather than philosophy
Russell considers the question undecidable
Russell praises him without qualification as the greatest of all philosophers
quiz.explanation: Russell states explicitly that because Aquinas does not follow the argument wherever it leads, but instead seeks support for conclusions already fixed by doctrine, he does not deserve to be ranked with the best philosophers of Greece or modern times.
quiz.related_concept: The individual human soul, intellect, and the rejection of Averroism

quiz.prompt: What example does Russell use to illustrate that Aquinas's rational ethical arguments are not fully sincere?
options: The argument for the indissolubility of marriage
The argument against astrology
The argument for the Trinity
The argument for papal supremacy
quiz.explanation: Russell notes that even if Aquinas's stated reasons for lifelong monogamy (paternal rationality and physical strength) were refuted, no Thomist would abandon the conclusion -- showing the real grounds lie elsewhere.
quiz.related_concept: The five (and related) proofs of God's existence

quiz.prompt: Aquinas resolves the puzzle of a lifelong cannibal's bodily resurrection by arguing that bodily identity does not require retaining the same matter.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Aquinas points out the body's matter is constantly replaced during ordinary life through digestion, so identity of body does not depend on identity of matter, resolving the cannibal puzzle.
